newsitem.title: USA: Browner targets big polluters to meet new air rule.
newsitem.headline: Browner targets big polluters to meet new air rule.

text.p: The top U.S. environmental official Thursday tried to reassure farmers and small businesses that they would not be hammered with new costs as states move to meet new smog and soot standards set this week.

"What we believe ... is that focusing on the largest sources, the combustion sources, the large utilities, you can get the kind of pollution reductions you need, and you can do it in the most cost-effective manner," said Environmental Protection Agency administrator Carol Browner.

Speaking at a Center for National Policy Breakfast, where labor, agriculture, and small business representatives raised concern about the economic costs of the strict new standards, Browner said imposing pollution controls on farms and small firms would not be the cheapest way to meet the standards.

"We're not going to do anything like that, I can assure you, and I would be surprised if you could find a governor or mayor who would do anything like that," she said. "It's just not going to happen."
Industry groups have complained that Browner has made those promises to other sectors, when in fact it will be up to states to decide how they plan to comply with the contrversial new air rules.

Utilities and manufacturers have estimated they will have to spend billions of dollars to curb smog-forming emissions, but Browner said cost predictions of meeting clean air standards in the past had all turned out to be too high.

She pointed to sulfur dioxide emissions cuts, which utilities had expected to cost $1000 per ton and EPA had pegged at $600 per ton, but have actually cost less than $100 per ton, with the help of an emissions credit trading scheme, technology improvements, and low sulfur coal supplies.

The administration believes the average cost of reducing each ton of smog-forming emissions will be $2500. Backing those claims, the Clinton administration set a $10,000 cap on the cost per ton of cutting emissions, EPA officials said.

If a plant that is required to reduce pollution can prove that it cannot find a way to do it for less than $10,000 per ton of emissions, either through trading pollution credits or using new technology, then it would have to contribute $10,000 per ton of targeted emissions to a fund.

State or local governments would use then use that money to buy cleaner technologies, such as alternative fuel vehicles for government fleets or more energy-efficient technologies for government buildings, to help reduce pollution.
"We're not convinced anyone will have to pay into (the fund)," EPA assistant administrator Fred Hansen told Reuters after Browner spoke.

According to a two-year study done by 37 eastern states, curbing pollution from power plants would cost $600 to $3500 per ton of emissions, while cutting smog-forming emissions from cars and trucks would cost at least $15,000 per ton.
